old: RC = +1, and the synthetic shows a full amplitude peak
new: RC = +1, and the synthetic shows a full amplitude peak, as it would at a perfect mirror

old: RC = -1, and the synthetic shows a full amplitude trough
new: RC = -1, and the synthetic shows a full amplitude trough, because the wave comes back inverted

old: Taking the difference between neighbouring reflection coefficients
new: Taking the difference between neighbouring reflection coefficients, so that the synthetic trace becomes the time derivative of the reflectivity series

old: Stretching one wavelet so that it spans the whole logged interval
new: Stretching one wavelet so that it spans the whole logged interval, then scaling that single stretched wavelet by the average reflection coefficient

old: Because a low frequency Ricker wavelet has a larger peak value than a high frequency one
new: Because a low frequency Ricker wavelet has a larger peak value than a high frequency one, so every event on the low frequency synthetic is scaled up before any summing takes place along the trace

old: Because the reflection coefficients themselves become larger when the frequency is lowered
new: Because the reflection coefficients themselves become larger when the frequency is lowered, since the impedance contrasts are averaged over a longer window and the averaged interfaces then reflect more strongly

old: Because 15 Hz shifts every reflector to a shallower two way time
new: Because 15 Hz shifts every reflector to a shallower two way time, where the overburden is thinner and the impedance contrasts between the shallower layers on this well are much sharper than they are deeper down

old: Two clearly separated events, each at its own correct time
new: Two clearly separated events, each at its own correct time, because the convolution keeps every reflection coefficient on its own sample of the time grid

old: The shallower of the two interfaces is dropped from the calculation
new: The shallower of the two interfaces is dropped from the calculation, since the engine keeps only one coefficient per wavelet length and retains the deeper one

old: An amplitude equal to the sum of the two impedances
new: An amplitude equal to the sum of the two impedances, because the synthetic adds the rock properties on either side of each interface into a single composite value

old: Resolution falls but amplitudes rise
new: Resolution falls but amplitudes rise, because the shorter wavelet blurs neighbouring reflectors together while its sharper peak carries more energy into every event

old: Both resolution and amplitude rise together
new: Both resolution and amplitude rise together, since a higher frequency wavelet is both shorter in time and brighter at its peak, so every event gains on both counts

old: Nothing changes, because the reflection coefficients are the same either way
new: Nothing changes, because the reflection coefficients are the same either way and the synthetic is fully determined by the reflectivity series whatever the wavelet

old: Mean gamma ray, mean neutron porosity, mean density, mean sonic, sample count and log step
new: Mean gamma ray over the logged interval, mean neutron porosity over the same interval, mean bulk density from the RHOB curve, mean sonic transit time from the DT curve, the count of finite samples used, and the depth step of the log

old: Wavelet frequency, wavelet length, side lobe value, peak value, sample rate and grid length
new: Wavelet frequency in hertz, wavelet length in milliseconds, the side lobe value of the Ricker, its central peak value, the sample rate of the time grid and the total grid length, all read from the wavelet and time grid settings

old: Mean velocity, mean density, mean impedance, mean reflection coefficient, mean amplitude and sample count
new: Mean velocity over the interval, mean density over the interval, mean acoustic impedance, the mean reflection coefficient across all interfaces, the mean synthetic amplitude along the trace and the count of finite samples behind them

old: They should be used to mark the top and the base of the logged interval
new: They should be used to mark the top and the base of the logged interval when the depth range is set

old: The synthetic was accidentally shifted by 60 ms during the depth to time conversion
new: The synthetic was accidentally shifted by 60 ms during the depth to time conversion, so every event on the trace now sits later than the interface that produced it and a bulk shift of the same size would simply realign them all

old: The reflection coefficient at 1642 ms must be larger than the one at 1582 ms
new: The reflection coefficient at 1642 ms must be larger than the one at 1582 ms, since the strongest amplitude on a synthetic always sits on the strongest single interface and the reported coefficient ranking has to be wrong

old: One of the two numbers is a reporting error, which the capstone tolerance absorbs
new: One of the two numbers is a reporting error, which the capstone tolerance absorbs, because a synthetic amplitude cannot peak anywhere except at the time of the largest reflection coefficient that drives it on the synthetic trace

old: That the wavelet frequency must always be raised to 40 Hz before tying
new: That the wavelet frequency must always be raised to 40 Hz before tying, because a sharper wavelet removes the lag and lets the events line up by eye

old: Module quizzes at 75 percent with no cooldown, the final exam at 75 percent, and the capstone first
new: Module quizzes at 75 percent with no cooldown, the final exam at 75 percent, and the capstone first, so the graded numbers are read before any module quiz is attempted

old: Seismic amplitudes are always too weak to pick without a well to boost them
new: Seismic amplitudes are always too weak to pick without a well to boost them into a usable event

old: Seismic surveys record depth directly, so the tie merely confirms the depths
new: Seismic surveys record depth directly, so the tie merely confirms the depths already on the section

old: Horizon mapping is done in the well domain, so seismic contributes nothing to it
new: Horizon mapping is done in the well domain, so seismic contributes nothing to it between the wells

old: The difference between velocity and density
new: The difference between velocity and density at each sample

old: The ratio of velocity to density
new: The ratio of velocity to density, measured in the rock matrix

old: The reciprocal of velocity multiplied by porosity
new: The reciprocal of velocity multiplied by porosity, sample by sample

old: The two-way time in milliseconds is always larger than the depth in metres
new: The two-way time in milliseconds is always larger than the depth in metres on the teaching well at every depth

old: Multiplying the two-way time by velocity returns the depth you started with
new: Multiplying the full two-way time by velocity returns the depth you started with at the well

old: The 2000 m/s is the measured rock velocity, and the 3145.29 m/s is the assumed overburden average
new: The 2000 m/s is the measured rock velocity, and the 3145.29 m/s is the assumed overburden average used only to hang the log on the time axis at the well

old: They are two estimates of the same quantity, and the more precise one should be preferred
new: They are two estimates of the same quantity, and the more precise one should be preferred, which makes the measured sonic average the one to carry through both the time axis and the impedance

old: By assuming the seismic sample interval matches the log sample interval
new: By assuming the seismic sample interval matches the log sample interval, so each log sample can be assigned the time of its matching seismic sample

old: By reading the two-way time straight off the seismic display at the well location
new: By reading the two-way time straight off the seismic display at the well location, where the strongest event is taken as the target top

old: Because the sonic log is recorded at exactly 2 ms intervals in the borehole
new: Because the sonic log is recorded at exactly 2 ms intervals in the borehole, so the synthetic has to inherit that step

old: Because uneven spacing would make the well tops land at odd millisecond values
new: Because uneven spacing would make the well tops land at odd millisecond values that the display cannot label

old: Because positive coefficients paint as peaks only above about 0.1 in magnitude
new: Because positive coefficients paint as peaks only above about 0.1 in magnitude, with weaker ones shown as troughs

old: Because the sign of the coefficient changes with the depth of the interface
new: Because the sign of the coefficient changes with the depth of the interface as the overburden compacts it

old: Because peaks and troughs are assigned at random by interpretation software
new: Because peaks and troughs are assigned at random by interpretation software each time a section is loaded

old: At 1580 ms, which is 1580 m under the teaching time to depth function
new: At 1580 ms, which is 1580 m under the teaching time to depth function on this well

old: The peak is a noise spike, because five consecutive samples share the same sign
new: The peak is a noise spike, because five consecutive samples share the same sign and a real event would change sign

old: Zero, so the trace stays continuous through the missing interval
new: Zero, so the trace stays continuous through the missing interval and the convolution can run unbroken

old: It guarantees the synthetic and the seismic have the same amplitude scale
new: It guarantees the synthetic and the seismic have the same amplitude scale, so the two traces can be compared without any normalisation

old: Replace each wavelet sample with the nearest reflection coefficient
new: Replace each wavelet sample with the nearest reflection coefficient, so the wavelet shape is resampled onto the reflectivity time grid before it is displayed

old: Average the reflectivity series over a window as long as the wavelet
new: Average the reflectivity series over a window as long as the wavelet, which smooths the coefficients into a band limited trace at the seismic frequency

old: A peak of about plus 0.02 with negative side lobes on either side
new: A peak of about plus 0.02 with negative side lobes on either side, as for any Ricker

old: Frequency changes the amplitude of the wavelet but not its length
new: Frequency changes the amplitude of the wavelet but not its length, so resolution stays the same whichever frequency is chosen

old: The 15 Hz result must be a processing error, since higher frequency should always be brighter
new: The 15 Hz result must be a processing error, since higher frequency should always be brighter for the same underlying reflectivity series

old: The time to depth function is 60 ms out and the synthetic needs a bulk shift
new: The time to depth function is 60 ms out and the synthetic needs a bulk shift, after which the strongest amplitude would land back on the strongest coefficient where it belongs

old: The strongest coefficient was excluded from the convolution because it is negative
new: The strongest coefficient was excluded from the convolution because it is negative, and the engine only convolves positive coefficients, so its wavelet copy never reaches the trace

old: The wavelet peak is offset from its centre by 60 ms
new: The wavelet peak is offset from its centre by 60 ms, so every event on the synthetic appears later than the interface that produced it and the brightest one inherits that delay

old: Because the wavelet delays every event by half its length
new: Because the wavelet delays every event by half its length, so the brightest point of the synthetic always lands later than the coefficient that caused it by that same fixed amount

old: Because reflection coefficients are computed in depth and amplitudes in time
new: Because reflection coefficients are computed in depth and amplitudes in time, so the two maxima are reported on different axes and only agree once the depth scale is converted

old: Because negative coefficients are plotted at the following sample
new: Because negative coefficients are plotted at the following sample, which pushes the brightest amplitude one step later than the coefficient whenever the strongest reflection is negative

old: Only the 15 Hz result is trustworthy, because its peak matches a real interface
new: Only the 15 Hz result is trustworthy, because its peak matches a real interface, so the higher frequency run should be discarded before any tie is attempted

old: Amplitude should be ignored, since only the reflectivity series is meaningful
new: Amplitude should be ignored, since only the reflectivity series is meaningful and everything the wavelet adds on top of it is an artefact of the chosen wavelet frequency

old: Destructive interference is harmless because cancelled events reappear at higher frequency
new: Destructive interference is harmless because cancelled events reappear at higher frequency, so any dim interval can be recovered simply by rerunning with a sharper wavelet

old: A polarity convention problem that will disappear when the sign is flipped
new: A polarity convention problem that will disappear once the sign is flipped on the seismic display

old: Mean sonic velocity, TWT at the top of the log, maximum impedance, the strongest reflection coefficient, the strongest synthetic amplitude and the recovered bulk shift
new: Mean sonic velocity, TWT at the top of the log, maximum impedance, the strongest reflection coefficient, the strongest synthetic amplitude and the recovered bulk shift from the cross-correlation scan against the seismic

new: Pass the final exam at 75 percent, then the module quizzes at 70 percent, then the capstone, so that the exam acts as the entry test and the module quizzes follow it as revision before the final gate opens

old: Read every lesson, pass each module quiz at 70 percent, then the capstone, with no final exam involved
new: Read every lesson, pass each module quiz at 70 percent, then the capstone, with no final exam involved, since the capstone itself stands in for the exam and grants the certification once the quizzes are cleared

old: Nothing, because the two always coincide when the wavelet is zero phase
new: Nothing, because the two always coincide when the wavelet is zero phase, since a symmetric wavelet centres every copy on its own coefficient and the brightest point must fall on the largest one

new: That the two-way factor has to be applied twice, once to each entry, because the coefficient time comes from the depth to time conversion while the amplitude time is read off the trace separately

old: Because the capstone grades the recovered lag alongside the other numbers
new: Because the capstone grades the recovered lag alongside the other numbers, so the planted value has to be fixed in advance for every learner to be marked against the same answer

old: A second sonic curve so the velocity can be averaged for redundancy
new: A second sonic curve so the velocity can be averaged for redundancy, which reduces the noise in the impedance log and therefore in every reflection coefficient and synthetic amplitude built from it

old: An automatic depth conversion of the whole seismic volume
new: An automatic depth conversion of the whole seismic volume, using the tied time to depth function from the well to move every trace from two way time into depth so the horizons can be mapped in metres

old: A null handling pass over the input curves before the impedance is formed
new: A null handling pass over the input curves before the impedance is formed, so that gaps in DT and RHOB are filled by interpolation and the reflectivity series runs unbroken through the whole logged interval
